1. Introduction

This guide helps local authorities and their schools forums plan their implementation of the local funding system for the 2027 to 2028 financial year.

2. Expiry or review date

This guidance is for the 2027 to 2028 funding year.

3. Who this guidance is for

The guidance is for:

local authorities

schools forums

4. Changes in 2027 to 2028

The Department for Education (DfE) has published the mainstream schools national funding formula (NFF) for 2027 to 2028. A summary of the formula is set out in the NFF policy document, with more detailed information available in the NFF technical notes. NFF changes that affect local formulae arrangements are also covered in this guidance.

4.1 Changes to the national funding formula

Key changes to the schools NFF in 2027 to 2028

The school budget support grant 2026 (SBSG 26) is being rolled into the schools NFF. The approach to rolling in this grant is very similar to how earlier grants were rolled into the 2026 to 2027 NFF. We have rolled in this grant in 3 ways, to reflect the 3 different ways in which schools attract funding through the NFF:

increasing the basic entitlement, free school meals Ever6 (FSM6) and the lump sum factor values for schools funded through the main formula factors (before protections)

increasing the minimum per pupil levels

increasing the baseline for each school, which is used to calculate funding protections for schools funded through the funding floor

We have recalculated the grant’s per-pupil and per-school funding rates on a full year equivalent basis before rolling them into the NFF.

To note that the SBSG 26 funding that has been allocated by local authorities for mainstream schools with special units or resourced provision (SURPs) will be rolled into local authorities’ high needs allocations in 2027 to 2028. Local authorities will be required to continue to pass this funding on to schools.

Additionally, funding for schools will be reduced to reflect the decrease to employer contribution rates for the teachers’ pension scheme (TPS) from 1 April 2027. The funding reduction will reflect the decreased cost at national level and therefore be cost neutral for public sector employers as a whole.

The adjustment in respect of pensions contributions will be incorporated into the schools NFF and the local funding formulae in the same 3 ways as SBSG 26 is being rolled in (but as a reduction instead of an addition):

through changes in basic entitlement, FSM6 and the lump sum factor values

changes in the minimum per pupil levels (MPPLs)

adjustments to the baseline

After incorporating the SBSG 26 and the teachers’ pension employer contributions funding adjustment into the NFF, factor value increases have been applied to all factor values in the schools NFF, and the funding floor has been set at 1%.

Changes to the central school services block (CSSB)

The centrally employed staff elements of SBSG 26 are being rolled into the CSSB for 2027 to 2028, with the SBSG 26 grant element recalculated on a full-year basis. The total funding has also been adjusted downwards to reflect the decrease to the teachers’ pension employer contributions from April 2027.

Historic commitments funding will continue to be reduced by 20% each year. As set out in the 2026 to 2027 operational guidance, that reduction is now being calculated in respect of the 2025 to 2026 baseline. This means that all this funding will be phased out over a 5-year period, except for when protections are applied.

4.2 Requirements on local formulae

Local authorities must continue to bring their own formulae closer to the schools NFF. They must move their local formula factor values at least a further 10% closer to the NFF (building on the movement towards the NFF made in 2026 to 2027), except where local formulae are already ‘mirroring’ the NFF. These criteria do not apply to:

rates

private finance initiative (PFI)

exceptional circumstances factors

Details of how we calculate the 10% move and how we define ‘mirroring’ for the purpose of the tightening criteria are given in section 8.2: methodology underpinning the 10% tightening requirement.

Local authorities have the freedom to set the minimum funding guarantee (MFG) in their local formulae between 0.5% and 1% per pupil .

4.3 Dedicated schools grant transfers

Local authorities continue to be able to transfer up to 0.5% of their schools block to other blocks of the dedicated schools grant (DSG), with schools forum approval. You can read further information in section 20: transfer between blocks.

A disapplication is required for any transfers above 0.5%, or any amount without schools forum approval. This applies to any transfers, even if an amount was agreed in previous years.

5. Mainstream school funding for special educational needs

5.1 Notional special educational needs budgets

Local authorities are required to identify a notional budget for their mainstream schools, which helps them comply with their duty to use their ‘best endeavours’ to meet the special educational needs (SEN) of their pupils. The notional SEN budget is not a separate budget but is identified within a maintained school’s delegated budget share, or an academy’s general annual grant, and is calculated by local authorities using their local mainstream schools funding formula factors.

We have updated the guidance to help local authorities review their notional SEN budget calculations and to help schools understand the intended use of the notional SEN budget. All local authorities should review this calculation each year alongside their local formula to make sure that their school’s notional SEN budget is a realistic amount for meeting the costs of additional SEN support up to £6,000 per pupil. Any shortfall in this notional budget for schools where a standardised calculation does not work can be met from additional high needs targeted funding. High needs top-up funding should be allocated in addition to the notional SEN budget for SEN provision costs (including support for pupils with education, health and care (EHC) plans) in excess of £6,000 per pupil.

Further guidance can be found in the notional SEN budget for mainstream schools: operational guide. Local authorities can also review other local authorities’ current notional SEN budget calculations in section 20 of the schools block funding formulae 2026 to 2027.

5.2 Inclusive mainstream fund

Over the 3 years of the spending period, from financial year 2026 to 2027 to financial year 2028 to 2029, the inclusive mainstream fund provides £1.6 billion to support mainstream schools and other education settings in the transition towards a reformed education system that is inclusive by design. Guidance for schools is available in the inclusive mainstream fund: support for school leaders guidance.

From December 2026, schools will be required to publish an inclusion strategy, explaining how they will deliver inclusive whole-school approaches and evidence-based support to meet the needs of their cohort, including pupils with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND). This activity will be funded by the school’s core funding allocations, including their notional SEN budget, and the inclusive mainstream fund.

5.3 Upfront SEND funding for mainstream schools

Subject to their proposal to raise the £6,000 threshold being approved by the Secretary of State for Education, local authorities can transfer funding from their high needs budget to the schools budget to provide whole-school, upfront SEND funding for mainstream schools. This funding is provided so that schools can cover additional SEND support costs above the existing £6,000 threshold from their budget share. The new threshold will be proposed by the local authority, in consultation with the schools forum, and approved by the Secretary of State for Education. Schools will be able to plan strategically how to invest the upfront funding to provide early, responsive and flexible support for their pupil’s needs.

The funding will be distributed predominantly through a ‘local SEND inclusion factor’ (which is an addition to the local funding formula). Local authorities may also wish to retain part of the funding in the high needs block to provide discretionary, targeted funding to schools with particularly high rates of SEND. More information is available in upfront funding for mainstream schools: creating a ‘local SEND inclusion formula.

The ‘local SEND inclusion factor’ is provided separately from the local funding formula and will not change the notional SEN budget. Schools should consider all SEND funding when planning resources and reporting inclusion activity in their inclusion strategy. This activity is funded through the school’s whole budget, including notional SEND, the inclusive mainstream fund and any upfront SEND funding.

6. Reviewing and consulting on the pre-16 formula

Local authorities must engage in open and transparent consultation with all maintained schools and academies in their area, as well as with their schools forum, about any proposed changes to their local funding formulae, including the principles adopted and any transfer of funds between blocks.

Any consultation should include a demonstration of the effect of modelling such changes on individual maintained schools and academies.

Local authorities also need to set out how their proposals meet the requirements to move the local formulae towards the NFF, if they are not already ‘mirroring’ the NFF.

Local authorities should communicate proposed formula changes to all bodies affected by the changes.

The local authority is responsible for making the final decisions on their formula. Each local authority’s process should ensure that there is sufficient time to gain political approval before the authority proforma tool (APT) deadline 21 January 2027.

Political approval means approval in line with the local authority’s local scheme of delegation, so this may be decisions made by the council cabinet, cabinet member or full council. The schools forum does not decide on the formula.

We expect local authorities will have ensured that they allowed sufficient time for wider consultation with schools, agreement by their schools forum, and political approval where they wish to transfer funding out of the schools block, or submit a disapplication request. Further information is included in section 20: transfer between blocks.

7. Disapplications

7.1 General, high needs, early years and schools block transfer requests

Under The School and Early Years Finance (England) Regulations, we allocate the DSG to local authorities to fund schools and early years establishments. We recognise situations will arise where local authorities have unusual circumstances where particular provisions of the regulations or conditions of grant are not appropriate. Where this occurs, local authorities can make what are known as disapplication requests to the Secretary of State for Education.

For 2027 to 2028, as previously communicated, we encouraged requests to be submitted by 16 November 2026. This deadline was necessary to enable us to provide timely answers via email to ensure local authorities can:

submit their APT by 21 January 2027

set their local funding formulae for 2027 to 2028

issue compliant maintained school budgets by the end of February 2027

A disapplication digital form is available and must be used for disapplication requests, including general, high needs, early years and schools block transfer requests. You can read further information and access the form via submit a local authority disapplication request.

Local authorities are required to comply with the duty under Section 149 of the Equality Act 2010 when making decisions about disapplication proposals. Section 149 places a duty on local authorities to have due regard to the need to eliminate unlawful discrimination, advance equality of opportunity and foster good relations when making decisions and delivering services. We expect local authorities to have considered, consulted and explained the specific equality impacts their proposals might have in the disapplication request.

If an Equality Impact Assessment has not been provided to support the disapplication request it will remain on hold until this has been made available.

Additional information on the process for specific requests is provided in more detail in relevant subsections of this guide.

The department will communicate its final decisions directly to each local authority that submits a disapplication request.

7.2 Transfer request for upfront funding for mainstream schools

Local authorities wishing to use the flexibility to provide upfront SEND funding to mainstream schools must submit a formal application using the form that DfE will provide. As previously communicated, requests were required to be submitted by 30 October 2026 . This is necessary to provide timely answers via email to ensure local authorities can submit their APT by 21 January 2027. More information is available in the guidance apply to provide upfront SEND funding to mainstream schools.

This activity will be permitted by an amendment to The School and Early Years Finance (England) Regulations which will allow approved local authorities to raise the per child threshold from £6,000 for school contributions towards additional SEN support costs.

Additional information on the process for the block transfer is provided in more detail in section 5: mainstream school funding for special educational needs and section 20: transfer between blocks.

8. Delegated funding

8.1 Local authority funding formula factors for 2027 to 2028

There are 15 allowable funding factors in 2027 to 2028. Most are compulsory for all local authorities.

Compulsory

Basic entitlement

Free school meals (FSM)

Free school meals Ever6 (FSM6)

Income deprivation affecting children index (IDACI)

Low prior attainment (LPA)

English as an additional language (EAL)

Pupil mobility

Sparsity

Lump sum

London fringe (compulsory for the eligible authorities)

Split sites

Minimum level of per-pupil funding for primary and secondary schools

Optional

Rates

PFI factor for schools with PFI contracts

Exceptional circumstances (with our agreement)

8.2 Methodology underpinning the 10% tightening requirement

We continue to require local authorities to move their local formula factor values at least 10% closer to the NFF factor value compared to the previous year, except where local formulae are already ‘mirroring’ the NFF. This requirement does not apply to the optional, locally determined factors.

For the tightening criteria, local factor values within 2.5% of the respective NFF values are deemed to be ‘mirroring’ the NFF. This means that local authorities which had factor values within +/- 2.5% of the NFF values in 2026 to 2027 will be allowed to set their 2027 to 2028 factor values anywhere within +/- 2.5% of the 2027 to 2028 NFF values. Likewise, no local authority will be required to move their factor values closer than +/- 2.5% of the 2027 to 2028 NFF because of the 10% tightening requirement.

The 10% movement is calculated such that local authorities are required to bring their local formula factor values 10% closer to the NFF, compared to the difference between the local factor value and the NFF value in 2026 to 2027. Worked examples are given in table 1 below.

For local authorities where an area cost adjustment (ACA) is applied, the comparison is made between the local factor values and the NFF factor values with the ACA applied. As such, the required movement towards the NFF is a movement to the NFF value, as adjusted by the ACA.

As part of the tightening requirement, local authorities are not allowed to ‘overshoot’ the NFF value by more than the 2.5% ‘mirroring’ threshold. As such, a local authority which had a local factor value below the NFF value in 2026 to 2027 should increase the local factor value in 2027 to 2028 to get closer to the NFF, but it cannot set the factor value more than 2.5% above the NFF value. Conversely, a local authority which had a local factor value above the NFF value in 2026 to 2027 cannot set that factor value more than 2.5% below the 2027 to 2028 NFF value. Table 1 shows 2 examples illustrating how the tightening criteria work in practice.

Table 1: the tightening criteria in practice

Local factor value in 2026 to 2027 NFF factor value in 2026 to 2027 (including ACA) NFF factor value in 2027 to 2028 (including ACA) Minimum allowable local factor value in 2027 to 2028 Maximum allowable local factor value in 2027 to 2028

£500 £1,000 £1,050 £600 - The minimum value is £450 less than the 2027 to 2028 NFF factor value. This is 10% less than the £500 difference in 2026 to 2027 £1,076.25 - The maximum value is 2.5% above the 2027 to 2028 NFF value

£1,300 £1,000 £1,050 £1,023.75 - The minimum value is 2.5% less than the 2027 to 2028 NFF value £1,320 - The maximum value is £270 above the 2027 to 2028 NFF value. This is 10% less than the £300 difference in 2026 to 2027

The allowable factor value ranges: 2027 to 2028 for each local authority have now been published.

Local authorities are not permitted to seek to disapply the tightening requirements. Instead, local authorities have a number of other options for managing any affordability constraints that occur as a result of these tightening requirements. All local authorities can make use of the 2.5% threshold for ‘mirroring’ the NFF by setting their factor values 2.5% below the NFF values (including the ACA uplift). Local authorities are also allowed to cap and scale back overall gains for individual schools to ensure affordability. If affordability constraints remain once these options have been exhausted, local authorities can also submit disapplications to the minimum per pupil levels (MPPLs) and the MFG.

8.3 Basic entitlement

This compulsory factor assigns funding based on individual pupils in reception to year 11 who are aged 4 and above at the start of the academic year. The number of pupils for each maintained school or academy is based on the October 2026 pupil census.

Funding is allocated according to a basic per-pupil rate.

There is a single rate for primary age pupils.

For key stage 3 and key stage 4, rates should be different as they are for the schools NFF.

The rates for primary, key stage 3 and key stage 4 pupils must be at least 10% closer to NFF values than their respective baseline values, subject to the 2.5% threshold for ‘mirroring’ the NFF.

Local authorities must add the rolled-in basic entitlement elements of the (annualised) SBSG 26 and take into account the teachers’ pension employer contributions funding adjustment to their per-pupil rates in 2027 to 2028. The allowable factor values for each local authority are calculated on that basis.

8.4 Free school meals

This is a compulsory factor.

For FSM, factor values must be at least 10% closer to NFF factor values than their baseline factor values, except where local formulae are already ‘mirroring’ the NFF values.

We measure eligibility for current FSM using the October census. Following the expansion of FSM at the start of the 2026 to 2027 academic year, there will be 2 categories of FSM:

targeted FSM

expanded FSM

Local authorities should apply the FSM factor to pupils in both of these groups. This will ensure that funding for the expansion of FSM to pupils in households in receipt of universal credit will be incorporated into the core funding that mainstream schools receive in 2027 to 2028.

Since the NFF operates with a longer funding lag than the local authorities’ funding formulae, local authorities will not receive funding for the expansion through the schools NFF in 2027 to 2028. To ensure that local authorities can afford to allocate funding for the FSM expansion through their local formulae, they will receive additional funding (at the same rate as that provided through the NFF) through their DSG schools block. This will reflect the increase in FSM-eligible pupils that they will have to fund through their local mainstream schools formula. This additional funding will be included within local authorities’ DSG allocations published in December 2026.

You can read further guidance on the expansion of FSM for local authorities, local authority maintained schools, academies and free schools.

8.5 Free school meals Ever6

This is a compulsory factor.

FSM6 factor values must be at least 10% closer to NFF factor values than their baseline factor values, except where local formulae are already ‘mirroring’ the NFF values.

Local authorities must add the rolled-in FSM6 entitlement elements of the (annualised) SBSG 26 and take into account the teachers’ pension employer contributions funding adjustment to their FSM6 rates in 2027 to 2028. The allowable factor values for each local authority are calculated on that basis.

In 2027 to 2028 FSM6 will encompass those previously eligible for FSM, as well as those eligible for targeted FSM following the expansion to FSM. Pupils who are only eligible for expanded FSM, and who were not eligible prior to the expansion, will attract funding through the FSM factor only.

8.6 Income deprivation affecting children index

This is a compulsory factor, and all IDACI bands must be used.

The IDACI measure uses 6 bands. Different values can be attached to each band, and different unit values can be used for primary and secondary within each band. The per pupil value for each band must be at least 10% closer to the NFF than the baseline values, except where local formulae are already ‘mirroring’ the NFF values.

The 2027 to 2028 NFF, as in the previous year, uses IDACI 2019 ranks to group each lower super output area (LSOA), an area with typically about 1,500 residents, into one of 6 bands of decreasing deprivation. Table 2 shows the requirement and ranks for each IDACI band.

8.7. Low prior attainment

This is a compulsory factor.

Factor values must be at least 10% closer to the NFF values than their baseline values, except where local formulae are already ‘mirroring’ the NFF values.

Local authorities must apply this factor for:

primary pupils identified as not achieving a good level of development in the early years foundation stage profile (EYFSP)

secondary pupils not reaching the expected standard in key stage 2 at reading, writing or maths

Since 2017 to 2018, we have weighted the LPA factor for secondary year groups so that year-on-year fluctuations in pass-rates do not disproportionately affect the distribution of funding through the LPA factor in the mainstream formula.

In 2027 to 2028, we will carry forward the weightings we used in 2026 to 2027 for the year 7 to year 10 cohorts, so they will apply to the year 8 to year 11 cohorts, respectively.

For the financial year 2027 to 2028, the weightings are :

pupils in year 7 in October 2026: 62%

pupils in year 8 in October 2026: 60%

pupils in years 9 in October 2026: 58%

pupils in years 10 in October 2026: 56%

pupils in years 11 in October 2026: 54%

The weightings will operate in the same way as in 2026 to 2027: the number of pupils identified as having LPA in the data will be multiplied by the relevant weighting to determine the number of pupils eligible for the factor for funding purposes.

Following the cancellation or incompleteness of EYFSP assessments in summer 2021 due to COVID-19, local authorities will not be able to use assessment data from this year in the low prior attainment factor in their local funding formulae. Instead, local authorities will use 2022 attainment data as a proxy for the missing assessments in 2021. This will be reflected in the APT, but is not relevant for the secondary LPA factor as the pupils who would have sat key stage 2 assessments in 2021 have now left key stage 4.

For schools that do not have a cohort which sat the EYFSP assessments in 2022, local authorities will use the schools’ LPA proportions from the 2026 to 2027 APT as a proxy for the missing assessments in 2021. This will be based on the overall primary LPA proportion for the schools in question.

In the pre-populated APT, we will use local authority average LPA ratios from the 2022 assessment if the 2026 to 2027 APT data described in the paragraphs above is not available. Where we have used local authority average LPA ratios as a proxy for the missing assessments in the APT, local authorities will be allowed to make amendments to this data where it is not deemed appropriate.

LPA funding is allocated to all pupils identified as not reaching the expected standard at the previous phase, regardless of their year group. Pupils who have not undertaken the assessment are given the overall average attainment score of their year group, so are taken into account when calculating a school’s LPA rate. For primary LPA, the ratio of eligible pupils is calculated from pupils in years 1 to 6. This ratio is then applied to all pupils in years reception to year 6. This ensures that reception pupils also attract LPA funding. For primary schools which only have reception pupils, the local authority average ratio will be used.

8.8. English as an additional language

This is a compulsory factor.

The factor values must be at least 10% closer to NFF values than their baseline values, except where local formulae are already ‘mirroring’ the NFF values. There can be separate unit values for primary and secondary.

Pupils identified in the October census with a first language other than English attract funding for 3 years after they enter the statutory school system.

8.9. Pupil mobility

This is a compulsory factor.

The factor values must be at least 10% closer to NFF values than their baseline values, except where local formulae are already ‘mirroring’ the NFF values.

The mobility factor allocates funding to schools with a high proportion of pupils who have an entry date in the last 3 years that is ‘not typical’. For year groups 1 to 11, ‘typical’ means that the first census on which a pupil is recorded as attending the school (or its predecessors) is the October census. ‘Not typical’ means that the first census a pupil is recorded as attending the school is a January or May census. For the reception year, ‘typical’ means that the first census is in October or January.

The mobility methodology involves tracking individual pupils using their unique pupil ID through censuses from the past 3 years. If the first census when the pupil was in the school was a January or May census, they are a mobile pupil. This excludes reception pupils who start in January. This methodology also excludes pupils who joined in the summer term after the May census, or pupils who joined in autumn before the October census.

To be eligible for mobility funding, the proportion of mobile pupils in a school must be above the threshold of 6%. A per pupil amount is then allocated in respect of all mobile pupils above that threshold.

8.10. Sparsity

This is a compulsory factor.

Factor values must be at least 10% closer to NFF values than their baseline values, except where local formulae are already ‘mirroring’ the NFF values. Different values can be set in local funding formulae across all phases, as long as they all move at least 10% closer to NFF values.

The sparsity factor allocates funding to schools that are remote, measured by sparsity distances, and are small, based on average year group size.

We measure sparsity distances using road distances. To calculate a school’s sparsity distance, we take all the pupils for whom it is the nearest compatible school and find the average shortest road distance from these pupils’ home postcodes to their second nearest compatible schools.

A school is eligible for sparsity funding in the NFF if:

its sparsity distance is equal to or above the main distance threshold, or above the tapered distance threshold

the average year group size (calculated as the APT-adjusted pupil count divided by number of year groups present at the school) is below the relevant size threshold

Table 3 shows the requirements for sparsity funding and the tapers.

Table 3: requirements for sparsity funding and the tapers

School phase Size threshold: maximum average number of pupils per year group Main distance threshold: minimum average distance to second nearest compatible school Distance taper threshold: minimum average distance to second nearest compatible school

Primary 21.4 2 miles 1.6 miles

Secondary 120.0 3 miles 2.4 miles

Middle 69.2 2 miles 1.6 miles

All-through 62.5 2 miles 1.6 miles

Local authorities can reduce the average year group size threshold or increase the distance threshold in their local funding formulae. The distance and group size taper thresholds remain optional in local funding formulae for 2027 to 2028.

Year group size taper

In the NFF, schools’ sparsity allocations are tapered according to average year group size, so that the smaller the school the greater the allocation. Schools with a sparsity distance equal to or greater than the main distance threshold (2 or 3 miles) and an average year group size of less than or equal to half the year group threshold receive 100% of the sparsity funding for their phase. See examples in annex 1: examples of how sparsity funding can be allocated. More information on the calculation of schools’ sparsity weightings and allocations is available in the NFF technical note.

Local authorities can adopt the same taper as the NFF. Alternatively, they can determine schools’ allocations by a ‘continuous’ year group size taper or a fixed sum. Unlike in the NFF methodology, the continuous taper means schools with an average year group size of half the year group threshold will not receive 100% of the sparsity funding for their phase. Instead, they will receive half the maximum. The fixed sum means all eligible schools will receive the exact same sparsity amount irrespective of their size.

Distance taper threshold

Schools with a sparsity distance between the distance taper threshold and the main threshold will attract some sparsity funding through the NFF. The amount depends on both their size and how far away their sparsity distance is from the main threshold. The closer the school’s sparsity distance to the main distance threshold, the greater their allocation.

The distance taper threshold is optional in local funding formulae for 2027 to 2028. Where used, it must be set 20% below the main distance thresholds used in local funding formulae, as in the NFF. It can be used irrespective of whether the NFF year group size taper, the continuous taper, or the fixed sum is used. The same principle applies across these methodologies, in that the further away the school is from the main threshold, the smaller their allocation. See annex 1: examples of how sparsity funding can be allocated for examples of use of the distance taper threshold.

Local flexibilities and applications

As mentioned, local authorities have some flexibility over the design of the sparsity factor in 2027 to 2028. Any changes can be made in the APT, and updates would be recalculated automatically. In addition, local authorities can make applications to us about very small, sparse secondary schools, as follows:

local authorities can make an application to us to include an exceptional circumstance of up to £50,000 for very small sparse secondary schools, which would otherwise be unable to attract sufficient funding to remain viable. Local authorities can only make an application for this where schools have:

pupils in years 10 and 11

350 pupils or fewer

a sparsity distance of 5 miles or more

We produce sparsity distances for all schools in the schools block dataset and make these available to local authorities.

If a school opens after the sparsity distances have been calculated, the local authority can make a disapplication request for the school. The process is the same for schools that are affected by neighbouring schools closing. We will not recalculate figures during the year in these situations.

An existing school, qualifying for sparsity funding, would not lose the funding in year if a new school opened nearby.

Local authorities should agree all disapplication requests with their schools forum before submitting to us for consideration.

8.11 Lump sum

This is a compulsory factor.

The factor values must be at least 10% closer to NFF values than their baseline values, except where local formulae are already ‘mirroring’ the NFF values.

Local authorities must add the rolled-in lump sum elements of the annualised SBSG 26 and take into account the teachers’ pension employer contributions funding adjustment to their local formula lump sums in 2027 to 2028. The allowable factor values for each local authority are calculated on that basis.

Local authorities can set a flat lump sum for all phases or differentiate the sums for primary and secondary schools.

All-through schools will receive the secondary lump sum value, and middle schools will receive a weighted average lump sum value based on the number of primary and secondary year groups in the school.

This worked example in table 4 shows how the lump sum amount for a middle school is calculated. In this example, the primary lump sum is set at £140,000, and the secondary lump sum is set at £150,000.

Table 4: calculation of the lump sum for a middle school

School phase rate Lump sum amount

3 year groups at primary rate ((3 divided by 5) × £140,000) £84,000

2 year groups at secondary rate ((2 divided by 5) × £150,000) £60,000

Total rate for all 5 year groups £144,000

This middle school has a total of 5 year groups: 3 year groups (years 4 to 6) attracting the primary rate, and 2 year groups (years 7 to 8) attracting the secondary rate.

Where schools have amalgamated during the financial year 2026 to 2027, they will retain 70% of the second lump sum for the financial year 2027 to 2028.

For example

Assuming a lump sum of £150,000, the additional payment would be £105,000 calculated as £150,000 × 0.7 = £105,000.

For mergers involving 3 or more schools or where merging schools would have received different lump sum amounts refer to the 2026 to 2027 APT guidance.

Local authorities can apply to us to reduce this in exceptional circumstances.

Where schools amalgamate after 1 April 2027, the new school will receive funding equivalent to the formula funding of the closing schools added together for the appropriate proportion of the year. This means that they receive the combined lump sums for the remainder of the year and 70% of the second lump sum in the following year, as outlined in the example above.

Local authorities may apply to provide a second year of protection. This needs to be discussed and agreed with the schools forum.

Applications must specify the level of protection sought, although in general we would not expect the additional protection to exceed 40% of the second lump sum. We will consider applications on a case-by-case basis.

8.12 London fringe

This factor is only applicable to Buckinghamshire, Essex, Hertfordshire, Kent and West Sussex. It is compulsory for these local authorities.

The purpose of this factor is to support schools that have higher costs because they are in the London fringe area, and where only part of the local authority is in this area. The multiplier should be applied to the 7 pupil-led factors, the lump sum factor, the sparsity factor and the split sites factor.

For 2027 to 2028:

local authorities which were not already using the ratio of the 2 area cost adjustments (ACAs) in 2026 to 2027 will be required to move at least 10% closer to that ratio

local authorities which used the ratio of the 2 ACAs in 2026 to 2027 will be required to continue to do so

The 2.5% ‘mirroring’ threshold does not apply to the fringe factor. This means that those local authorities which used the ratio of the ACAs in 2026 to 2027 must continue to do so exactly in 2027 to 2028, without a 2.5% margin. It also means that those local authorities which are required to move 10% closer to the ACA ratios must not ‘overshoot’ and set a fringe multiplier which exceeds the ACA differential.

8.13 Split sites

The split sites factor is compulsory for all local authorities, ensuring that split sites funding will be allocated consistently and fairly across the country. Local authorities are required to set their split sites factor values within the 2.5% ‘mirroring’ threshold for the NFF.

The factor is made up of 2 parts, both of which are compulsory:

basic eligibility funding: schools must be allocated a lump sum payment for each of their additional eligible sites (up to a maximum of 3)

distance funding: additional funding must be paid out on top of the basic eligibility lump sum for schools whose eligible sites are separated by more than 100 metres (by road distance) from the main site

The basic eligibility criteria for split sites funding requires additional sites to:

be separated from the school’s main site by a public road or railway, and

have a building on them which is maintained by the school, and which is used for the education of 5 to 16-year-old pupils in mainstream education more than 50% of the time. This excludes playing fields, ancillary buildings and buildings leased out full time by the school to another entity

Further details on the eligibility criteria are set out in annex 5: split site eligibility criteria.

Funding for the distance element should be allocated through a tapered approach, beginning at 100 metres, with allocations increasing linearly up to 500 metres, from which point schools should receive the total maximum funding allowed.

The NFF lump sum for basic eligibility is £56,800 and the NFF maximum distance funding is £28,400. Local authorities are required to uplift these values with their respective ACAs in their local formulae and set their local factor values within the 2.5% ‘mirroring’ threshold of the ACA uplifted lump sum value. (For local authorities in the London fringe area, the relevant ACA as regards the split sites factor value will be the lowest ACA that applies within the local authority).

The number of additional sites that schools can receive funding for is capped at 3 per school. If a school has more than 3 additional sites, the distance funding should be calculated based on the 3 that are furthest away from the main site.

This should be done as changes occur throughout the year, to ensure that our record of eligible split sites is correct and up to date. We will then assess eligibility accordingly and provide subsequent distance calculations if eligible.

Information on changes to split site eligibility should be sent to FundingPolicy.Queries@education.gov.uk. We do not assess eligibility for split site funding based on proposals or forecasts. The sites must be in operation at the time you are contacting us.

Any not received and agreed in time for inclusion in the APT before it is released will need to be manually added to the APT by the local authority subject to approval. Check your APT on receipt to confirm if your approved split site is included.

In line with other factors in the schools NFF, and local authority formulae, funding for split sites will be lagged. Funding changes for new eligible sites will be made annually as part of the usual APT process. Schools should receive funding in the following year based on their split sites’ eligibility at the time of the APT deadline in January.

For example

If a school starts using a new eligible site at the start of an academic year, that site should be included in the following year’s APT. As a result, funding will flow through from the start of the following financial year for maintained schools, and the following academic year for academies. Conversely, where changes to school estates happen in-year, leading to a school losing a site, the school should continue to receive split sites funding for the remainder of that financial year (or academic year for academies).

Exceptions to this are:

Mergers and amalgamations

Where a school becomes eligible for split site funding as a result of a merger or an amalgamation, the relevant split sites funding should come into effect once the school no longer receives the 70% of the second lump sum in the financial year after the amalgamation. (However, if a local authority chooses to support the school with 40% of a second lump sum in the second financial year after the amalgamation, the school will benefit from both that and split site funding in that year).

De-amalgamations

In the case of de-amalgamations, where the 2 new schools will each receive a lump sum with immediate effect, any funding previously attracted through the split sites factor, which the new separate schools are no longer eligible for, should cease immediately. This is to ensure schools are not funded for both an additional lump sum and split sites funding at the same time.

Funding for split sites through the 2027 to 2028 NFF to local authorities will be based on our recorded list of eligible schools following our June 2026 deadline. Every year, we will notify local authorities of the deadline for updates to the list ahead of the NFF publication.

As it is the responsibility of local authorities to inform us of schools’ split site eligibility, for both maintained schools and academies, we recommend that local authorities issue a request to all schools in the local authorities twice a year for information on any changes in split site eligibility: firstly, ahead of the deadline for inclusion in the NFF, and secondly, ahead of the deadline for inclusion in the APT. Failure to notify us of eligible split sites can result in the local authority having to fund the site through its local formula, without receiving commensurate funding through the NFF.

8.14 Minimum per pupil level for primary and secondary schools

This is a compulsory factor. It must be used in local funding formulae, at the NFF values. No ACA is applied to this variable.

The purpose of this factor is for local authorities to provide the NFF minimum per pupil levels (MPPLs) to every school. All local authorities must implement the MPPLs by following the same methodology used in the NFF, as detailed in the NFF technical note.

For all schools, the calculation for a school’s individual minimum per-pupil level (MPPL) is:

(number of primary year groups × £5,050 + (number of key stage 3 year groups × £6,294) + (number of key stage 4 year groups × £6,909)

divided by

total number of year groups

This provides per-pupil funding of £5,050 for each primary school, and £6,540 for each secondary school with standard structures of 7 and 5 year groups, respectively. For middle schools, all-through schools, and other schools with a non-standard year group structure, this will produce a specific minimum per-pupil value that relates to the number of year groups in each phase.

When calculating the MPPLs for individual schools, local authorities should take the number of year groups from the APT, which is the approach taken in the NFF. When completing the APT, local authorities should only list the number of year groups in each key stage which have pupils in them at present or will do so in the upcoming year. Where a school will have empty year groups in the upcoming year, for example, a school which has recently opened, these should not be included in the APT.

The only factors not included in per-pupil funding for the purpose of the MPPL calculation are the premises factors (split sites, rates, PFI and exceptional circumstances). Any prior year adjustments local authorities have made must also be excluded from the calculation.

Any capping and scaling cannot take a school’s per-pupil funding below the MPPLs. The only further calculation that local authorities can make once their formula has provided the minimum levels is, for maintained schools only, to deduct funding for de-delegated central services if the schools forum has agreed this can be taken from their budget shares in 2027 to 2028. It should be noted that the risk protection arrangement (RPA) is also exempt from the MPPLs.

Local authorities have the option, as with other aspects of the school funding regulations, to request to disapply the use of the full NFF MPPL values. Such requests can be made on the grounds of affordability, including in relation to the circumstances set out in the final paragraph relating to the tightening of local formulae within section 8.2: methodology underpinning the 10% tightening requirement. Local authorities can also request to disapply MPPLs in relation to block movements. You can read further information in section 20: transfer between blocks.

Disapplication requests may also be submitted to alter the NFF methodology, for specific schools only, where the local authority can show that the relevant MPPL value for that school is skewed significantly by unusual year group sizes.

For example

A local authority may want to provide a higher MPPL for an all-through school with significantly larger secondary than primary year group sizes.

8.15 Rates

This is an optional factor.

In 2027 to 2028 it remains optional for billing authorities to implement the central national non-domestic rates (NNDR) payment process where we pay the NNDR bills on behalf of local authority maintained schools and academies. All local authorities were required to enter an estimate for their 2026 to 2027 NNDR in the 2026 to 2027 APT. This has informed the NFF NNDR funding for 2027 to 2028.

For local authorities, whose billing authority is not on the central payment system, any adjustments to 2025 to 2026 rates (or inflationary increases to 2026 to 2027 rates) amounts included in the 2026 to 2027 APT have also formed part of the 2027 to 2028 NFF NNDR allocation. NFF NNDR funding for these local authorities also remains lagged, as in previous years.

Local authorities implementing the central NNDR payment process for April 2027:

must upload their schools rates data for April 2027 to March 2028 to the NNDR online portal between 1 April 2027 and 22 May 2027 (these dates are provisional and subject to change)

can submit adjustment claims to schools rates bills for 2027 to 2028 using the NNDR online portal from 23 May 2027 to 29 January 2028 (these dates are provisional and subject to change)

We will confirm the payment process for April 2027 to billing authorities in December 2026.

NNDR payments will be made to billing authorities in June 2027, October 2027 and March 2028.

Rates should continue to be reflected in the section 251 (s251) outturn statement, and in each school’s accounts.

All state funded schools will retain liability for their own business rates, except for community and voluntary controlled schools for which liability will continue to rest with the local authority. Liable parties will continue to retain responsibility for the payment of any penalty charges incurred because of late or non-payment in instances where they are at fault, for example, if an academy converter fails to inform their billing authority of their conversion.

For those local authorities, whose billing authority is adopting the central payment process where a late or missed payment arises because of our error, the responsibility of schools (or local authorities for community or voluntary controlled schools) for payment of any resulting penalty charges is waived and we will cover any penalty charges incurred. Examples of such cases could include late payment due to processing delays or data upload failure.

For local authorities, whose billing authority decides they are not adopting the central NNDR payment process for April 2027, there are no changes to the existing NNDR arrangements.

Local authority DSG allocations will include the 2027 to 2028 NFF NNDR amount. Local authorities should include the 2027 to 2028 NFF NNDR amount in schools’ budgets. Further information is available in the 2026 to 2027 APT guidance.

NNDR adjustments due to revaluations for 2026 to 2027 will be submitted in the 2027 to 2028 APT by local authorities not on the centralised payments system. For local authorities, whose billing authority is on the central payments process, we only expect to see adjustments such as revaluations in the 2027 to 2028 APT which occurred in the last quarter of 2025 to 2026 (January 2026 to March 2026) and were not included in the 2026 to 2027 APT. Any prior year 2026 to 2027 adjustments for local authorities whose billing authority has implemented the centralised payment process will have been paid in-year, as we pay the actual bill.

In 2-tier local authorities, all billing authorities need to agree to implement the central payment process. If mutual consent is not reached it will not be possible for any billing authority to adopt the central payment process.

8.16 Private finance initiative contracts

This is an optional factor.

The PFI factor is typically used to cover situations where funding for the PFI ‘affordability gap’ is passed through to schools, and where schools then pay it back to the local authority. It can also cover situations where schools face unavoidable extra premises costs related to the PFI contracts, over and above what other schools face.

The main purpose of the factor is to cover additional costs related to the cost of building the schools themselves.

Revenue costs, such as for facilities management and energy, are costs which all schools face. These costs are covered by the funding schools receive from the other formula factors in their local authority’s funding formula and would not normally constitute a valid reason for additional funding through the PFI factor. We would only consider limited funding to support these costs on a case-by-case basis in extreme cases where it can be shown that these costs are excessively high, and the excessive costs cannot be renegotiated. Agreement must be sought from us before any funding for such revenue costs is included in the PFI factor.

Methodologies for funding PFI schools must be objective and clear, and capable of being replicated for academies. There may be different arrangements between contracts but, within a contract, all PFI schools should be treated on a consistent basis.

For each PFI project where there is a PFI factor, local authorities are expected to have an affordability model covering the whole term of the PFI scheme (typically 25 to 30 years) to substantiate the amount of funding allocated through the PFI factor. We reserve the right to ask to see and review these models.

The PFI funding that local authorities receive through the NFF is calculated as the lower of:

the previous year’s PFI factor allocation in the NFF, uprated by Retail Price Index excluding mortgage interest payments (RPIX)

the previous year’s PFI factor allocation in the local formula, uprated by RPIX

Note that this calculation is done at the level of individual schools. As such, for schools whose 2026 to 2027 APT values were above the 2026 to 2027 NFF values, the lower NFF values have been used in the calculation of the 2027 to 2028 NFF values.

Conversely, for schools whose 2026 to 2027 APT values were below the 2026 to 2027 NFF values, the lower APT values have been used in the calculation of the 2027 to 2028 NFF values. This is likewise the approach that we plan to take in the 2028 to 2029 NFF, where we plan to calculate the PFI factor based on the lower of 2027 to 2028 NFF and 2027 to 2028 APT values.

Local authorities wishing to receive a higher NFF uplift need to apply to us, accompanied by a clear affordability model to substantiate the requested increase. This should be sent to: FundingPolicy.Queries@education.gov.uk.

Any remaining reserves at the end of the contract will need to be returned to us, as we would not fund anything through the PFI factor which is beyond what the local authority needs to cover the affordability gap and any unavoidable extra premises costs.

Where PFI factor values entered in the APT exceed those in the NFF, the local authority should consult its schools forum as part of the local formula consultation. Given the impact on the overall schools block and the consequent reduction in funding available to other schools, any uplift should be clearly justified and transparently presented. That is because such values would not be funded through the NFF the following year without a supporting acceptable PFI affordability model and would therefore have an impact on how much funding is available to spend elsewhere.

For PFI contracts which come to an end part way through a financial year, the PFI factor value entered on the APT should correspond to the funding required up until the end of the contract.

For example

For a contract expiring 31 August 2027, we would expect the PFI factor valued to be pro-rated for 5 months of the 2027 to 2028 financial year.

You can read further information on the PFI factor in the additional guidance published alongside this operational guide.

8.17 Exceptional circumstances

This is an optional factor.

Local authorities may apply for an exceptional circumstances factor where costs relating to school premises are exceptional, unavoidable and specific to a small number of schools. The costs should arise from circumstances that cannot reasonably be reflected through the standard funding formula factors and should not represent general operating costs incurred by schools.

Examples may include rental costs or contractual arrangements relating to shared or jointly used facilities.

Local authorities should only submit applications where the:

cost exceeds 1% of the individual school’s budget share

factor applies to fewer than 5% of schools within the local authority’s area

The 1% threshold applies to the individual school’s budget share before the exceptional circumstances factor is applied. Local authorities should provide calculations demonstrating that the relevant costs exceed this threshold.

Local authorities should also provide evidence of the number of schools affected and demonstrate that these represent fewer than 5% of schools within the authority.

Local authorities must submit requests annually for approval. Even where approval was granted in 2026 to 2027, local authorities must reapply if the criteria continue to be met.

Local authorities should submit requests for all exceptional circumstance factors in 2027 to 2028, with supporting evidence, by the disapplication deadline, setting out the rationale for the factor and demonstrating how the criteria are met.

The deadline for local authorities to submit requests for exceptional circumstances was 16 November 2026. This is to ensure decisions are communicated to local authorities before the authority proforma tool (APT) submission deadline.

Disapplications received after this deadline will still be considered. However, a decision prior to APT submission cannot be guaranteed.

Exceptional circumstances that have previously been approved include:

rents

joint use of leisure facilities by contractual agreement

building schools for the future schemes (additional contribution to lifecycle maintenance costs)

hire of PE facilities

a school with a farm included as part of its educational provision

These examples illustrate circumstances that have previously been approved. Inclusion in this list does not indicate that future applications will be approved. Each application will be considered on its own merits and based on the evidence provided.

The following costs will not normally be approved because they represent common operational costs faced by schools or costs that can be accommodated through other elements of the funding system:

utility costs for any type of building

funding leases for costs other than delivering education

circumstances where costs to the school do not exceed 1% of its budget share

rental costs for local authority-owned facilities, whether managed by the local authority or by a third party, that are used for the purpose of delivering the curriculum

any costs relating to swimming pools

Supporting evidence must be provided with all requests and, for service level agreements, licenses and rental agreements, we will require:

in-date agreements

agreements confirming revenue costs

confirmation of hours and the facilities/premises being used

details of the premises

current invoices

where a formal lease has expired but remains in effect through a rolling tenancy, periodic tenancy or similar continuing arrangement, evidence of the current rental charge and any increase in rental costs for which funding is being requested

Contact LA.Disapplications@education.gov.uk with any questions about a school’s eligibility.

We will contact local authorities if the evidence provided is insufficient. However, failure to provide the necessary supporting evidence may result in the disapplication request being rejected.

Local authorities are not obliged to request additional factors, but in considering whether to do so, they should look at the exceptional circumstances of academies and free schools as well as maintained schools.

9. Variations to pupil numbers

Local authorities are no longer expected to request approval from us to increase the pupil numbers used for calculating funding for specific schools where:

there has been, or is going to be, a reorganisation

a school has changed, or is going to change, its admission limit

However, we expect local authorities to present any pupil variations to their schools forum, to illustrate the impact to overall funding, and on specific schools’ budgets.

We want to continue to provide protection for all schools, including those where pupil numbers fall between census counts from one year to the next. This means that any request for a negative adjustment still requires a disapplication and compelling evidence to support it. Other increases not falling within these categories would require a disapplication request.

Where a new school is due to open, local authorities must estimate the pupil numbers expected to join the school in September and fund accordingly, explaining the rationale underpinning the estimates.

Under the regulations, local authorities must estimate pupil numbers for all schools and academies, including free schools, where they have opened in the previous 7 years, and are still adding year groups. Local authorities can adjust estimates each year, to take account of the actual pupil numbers in the previous funding period. You can read further information in section 32: treatment in the APT of new and growing schools.

All mainstream free schools are recoupable from the first year of opening. This means we will provide funding directly to the free schools opening, and recoup the funding from local authorities from the estimated pupil numbers in the APT.

Whilst the growth fund is a suitable route for short-term increases in pupil numbers and bulge classes, local authorities should vary pupil numbers in situations where the scale of change in numbers is sufficiently great and permanent that it should be applied to all factors in the formula.

If pupil numbers are not adjusted upwards to reflect actual intake, we will adjust amounts recouped to enable us to properly fund academies and free schools affected by this.

You can read further information in the flowchart at annex 2: funding for growing schools about when to request a variation, and when to use the growth fund. A text version of the flowchart is at annex 2a: funding for growing schools.

10. Minimum funding guarantee

Local authorities will continue to set a pre-16 MFG in their local formulae, to protect schools from excessive year-on-year changes.

Local authorities will be able to set an MFG between 0.5% and 1.0% per pupil compared to the baseline. Any local authorities wanting to set an MFG outside of these parameters must submit a disapplication request. Applications to set a lower MFG than 0.5% will only be considered on the grounds of affordability where local authorities have already exhausted the flexibility available from the 2.5% threshold for ‘mirroring’ the NFF as well as capping and scaling, see final paragraph within section 8.2: methodology underpinning the 10% tightening requirement.

Local authorities must include funding representing the funding allocated through the annualised SBSG 26 and take into account the teachers’ pension employer contributions funding adjustment in respect of their reception to year 11 pupils into the baseline. This includes the basic per-pupil, FSM6 and lump sum components. The required adjustment will be included in the APT when it is made available to each local authority. The funding adjustments made to the baseline are based on pupil numbers from the APT itself rather than the pupil numbers underpinning the actual SBSG 26 allocations. That is to ensure that changes in pupil numbers do not distort the funding protected through the MFG in per pupil terms.

Local authorities need to consult on any changes to the level of the MFG, as with the rest of the formula.

The MFG applies to pupils in reception to year 11. Early years pupils and post-16 pupils are excluded from the calculation.

The following elements of funding must be added to schools’ budget shares before the MFG calculation:

funding deducted through the negative factor for schools entered into the risk protection arrangement as set out in the school finance regulations

funding for de-delegated services that have been agreed with the schools forum under regulations as set out in the school finance regulations

negative adjustments for excluded pupils during the year as set out in the school finance regulations

The following elements of funding are automatically excluded from the MFG calculation, as not doing so would result in excessive protection, or would be inconsistent with the school finance regulations:

the 2027 to 2028 lump sum: this is excluded from both the baseline and 2027 to 2028 funding so that schools are protected against significant change in the lump sum between years

any higher lump sum paid under the regulations in 2026 to 2027 for amalgamated schools: this is excluded from the baseline only

any higher lump sum to be paid under the regulations in 2027 to 2028 for amalgamating schools: this is excluded from the 2027 to 2028 funding only

the 2027 to 2028 sparsity factor: this is excluded from both the baseline and 2027 to 2028 funding so that schools are protected against significant change in the sparsity value between years

rates: these are excluded from both the baseline and 2027 to 2028 funding, at their respective values for each year

any positive adjustments for excluded pupils during the year as set out in the school finance regulations

split sites funding: this is excluded from both the baseline and 2027 to 2028 funding, at their respective values for each year (this includes any London fringe uplift funding applied to the split sites funding in relevant local authorities) - this exclusion ensures that funding increases and decreases in line with split site eligibility resulting from changes to the school estate

PFI funding: this is excluded from both the baseline and 2027 to 2028 funding, at their respective values for each year - this ensures that changes in PFI funding do not impact on other aspects of school funding

The requirements for the MFG calculation are set out in detail in the school finance regulations.

The school finance regulations relating to the MFG allow for technical adjustments. These do not need authorisation from the Secretary of State for Education but will need to be shown and explained in the tables contained within the APT. They include:

where a budget was held centrally in the previous financial year and has now been delegated - this could include services that were previously funded centrally but have now been delegated, or additional funding released to schools as historic commitments have ended

transfer of funding from the schools block to the high needs block, but only where the high needs block is now responsible for funding amounts that had previously been met by a school’s delegated budget - in other words, there is a transfer of funding responsibility, not just a transfer of funding between blocks to meet cost pressures

All other funding will be in the MFG baseline and there will be no other automatic adjustments. Local authorities can, however, exclude other premises factors from the MFG without a disapplication, if they wish to ‘mirror’ the NFF.

All approvals to disapply the MFG for 2026 to 2027 were specific to that year and we do not expect these to be repeated. We will not carry forward any previous approvals.

The deadline, as previously communicated, for local authorities to submit any applications to disapply the MFG for 2027 to 2028 was 16 November 2026, for them to be considered and decisions provided prior to the APT submission deadline.

The disapplication digital form continues to be used for all disapplication requests. It is important that local authorities use this route for submitting requests. This will enable us to process and understand the details of each request more quickly.

Applications to disapply the MFG for individual schools will only be considered if there is a significant change in a school’s circumstances or pupil numbers. We will only consider requests where the inclusion of a factor in the MFG will lead to significant inappropriate levels of protection. Local authorities should provide detailed information on the financial impact of any request.

Examples of MFG disapplication requests that have been approved previously include:

where the normal operation of the MFG would produce perverse results for very small schools with falling or rising rolls

secondary schools that are admitting primary age pupils who would otherwise be over protected at the secondary age weighted pupil unit of funding

where over protection would otherwise occur, for example, where additional funding has been distributed in the previous year and the local authority can demonstrate that the funding is genuinely one-off
